subjects.displayTitle: House of Worship: a gathering place for prayer and service
subjects.introduction: At dawn someone walks toward a building, thoughts centred on God, and sits down in silence to listen. Bahá’u’lláh blesses that walker and commands that such houses be raised throughout the lands in the name of the Lord of all religions, adorned without images. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá widens the doorway until every race and sect can pass through it, then keeps building outward: a hospital, a hospice for the traveller, a school for orphans, a university, charities dispensed without regard to colour, so that worship and science may shower their gifts on one humanity. He insists that wherever a heart sincerely prays there is already a Mashriqu’l-Adhkár, and he delights in an aged believer carrying stones morning and evening, in a composer’s melody, in a vow of fifty tumans, in a gathering given another name when caution required it. What does a life become when stillness before God flows into care for neighbours? The question continues into devotional gatherings and feasts, into music and singing, and into the humanitarian work through which a community is built.

shortened: The House of Worship forms the central edifice of the Mashriqu'l-Adhkar (the Dawning-place of the Praise of God), a complex which, as it unfolds in the future, will comprise in addition to the House of Worship a number of dependencies dedicated to social, humanitarian, educational, and scientific pursuits. 'Abdu'l-Baha describes the Mashriqu'l-Adhkar as "one of the most vital institutions in the world", and Shoghi Effendi indicates that it exemplifies in tangible form the integration of "Baha'i worship and service". Anticipating the future development of this institution, Shoghi Effendi envisages that the House of Worship and its dependencies "shall afford relief to the suffering, sustenance to the poor, shelter to the wayfarer, solace to the bereaved, and education to the ignorant".
